sentences.text: Europelta was a medium-sized dinosaur estimated to reach about 5 meters in length and weigh 1.3 tonnes, though some estimates suggest a length closer to 4.5 meters.
This animal is distinguished by a quadrate bone that is shorter and wider than in any other ankylosaur.
The sacrum of Europelta is arched dorsally by 55 degrees.
The skull of Europelta is approximately 370.3 mm long and 299.1 mm wide, narrowing to 203.7 mm at the rear.
Europelta possessed amphicoelous vertebrae that were wider than they were tall and constricted in the middle.
Like other nodosaurids, Europelta had a foot with four pedal phalanges.
Europelta is the largest known member of the dinosaur clade Struthiosaurini.
The femoral head of Europelta is angled at approximately 115 degrees relative to the femur's long axis.
The tibia of Europelta features a broadly rounded cnemial crest.
Hollow, plate-like osteoderms with sharp edges ran down the sides of Europelta's tail and decreased in size rapidly.
The genus Europelta was described by Kirkland and colleagues in 2013, with the species Europelta carbonensis named by the same group.
Two partial skeletons of Europelta were discovered in 2011.
The holotype and paratype specimens of Europelta were found with abundant osteoderms, but these were not preserved in their original positions relative to the skeleton.
Microfossils indicate that the habitat was a permanent freshwater lake.
The fossil-bearing layer consists of dark olive-gray to olive-black mudstone preserving a high percentage of fossil plant debris.
Evidence of fused fern lamellae and abundant charcoal indicates the area was affected by a wildfire.
Heavy rainfall likely moved charred remains downstream where they were later buried in a nearby depositional area.
Europelta is a monospecific genus of nodosaurid dinosaur found in Spain.
Descriptores placed Europelta in Nodosauridae, forming the smaller clade Struthiosaurinae with the European nodosaurids Anoplosaurus, Hungarosaurus, and Struthiosaurus.
Europelta lived during the mid-Cretaceous, specifically the early Albian stage, approximately 113 million years ago, with a range from 113.2 to 110.1 million years ago.
It is debated whether Europelta belongs to Struthiosaurinae, as the original classification lacked a phylogenetic analysis.
Researchers disagree on Europelta's closest relatives, with some studies placing it as sister to Pawpawsaurus and others including Borealopelta in that relationship.
Some phylogenetic analyses place Europelta in a polytomy with Struthiosaurus, Stegopelta, Hungarosaurus, and Pawpawsaurus.
Other studies suggest Europelta is the sister taxon to Hungarosaurus.
